title: Rama refuses to blame
hookLine: everyone in the palace wants someone to blame, and Rama won't

lines: BLAME CAN BECOME ITS OWN FIRE.
cards: Who did this? In Ayodhya today, three answers are ready: Kaikeyi, Manthara, the king. Knowing who's responsible matters; it's how a wrong gets named and mended.

But a hunt for blame can become its own fire, and burn longer than the thing that started it. Lakshmana is already reaching for the names. Rama is the one person with every right to say them out loud.

teach.b: Lakshmana is still burning, and Rama speaks to him directly. Put away the things gathered for the coronation, he says, and help me get ready to go. Then, surprisingly, he talks about Kaikeyi.
Don't blame her. She has never treated me differently from her own son. If she has suddenly asked for this, cruel as it is, something larger than her is at work.

His word is daiva, what comes from the gods, what we'd call fate or destiny. No one can fight what is given this way, he says. Happiness and sorrow, gain and loss, birth and death: they come, and nobody fully knows why.
It could sound like giving up.

teach.h: TAKING THE HATRED OUT OF THE ROOM.
teach.b: But look at what it does in the story: it takes the hatred out of the room. Rama isn't saying Kaikeyi did nothing. He's refusing to make her the enemy, because she was once a mother to him and may be again.
Lakshmana will argue the other side soon, and Valmiki will let him. Today, notice just this: Rama uses the idea to protect someone who has hurt him.

teach.h: A WEEK: A PLAN, A PROMISE, A CALM.
teach.b: And the week behind us: a maid's plan, an old promise claimed, a king's night of pleading, a father who could only say his son's name, and three days of Rama's calm.
Dharma before the crown, kindness with his mother, and now daiva: no enemy made of Kaikeyi.

how: Sanskrit texts name two forces, daiva, fate or what the gods give, and purushakara, human effort; in the Ramayana the two sides are spoken by two brothers, Rama here and Lakshmana soon after.

o: his refusal to blame Kaikeyi, calling it daiva
his plan to punish Manthara once he returns
a fear of Kaikeyi that keeps him quiet

games.q: no one to blame — tap the pairs.
p: treated Rama like her own son
Rama asks for them to be put away

s: Rama blames Kaikeyi for the exile
he tells Lakshmana not to blame her; something larger is at work.
Rama uses the idea of daiva to protect someone who hurt him
it takes the hatred out of the room.
Valmiki lets fate have the last word here
Lakshmana will soon answer Rama, arguing for human effort.

games.q: you're Rama. your brother wants to name and punish the person who did this. what do you say?
o: Kaikeyi did this; she'll answer for it.
don't blame her; this is daiva.
games.why: Rama refuses to make Kaikeyi the enemy: she treated him like a son, and what happened is larger than her.

practice: Think of someone you've been blaming, for something large or small, and picture their face. Without deciding they were right, try to see them as Rama saw Kaikeyi: someone once kind to you, who might be again.
Breathe out, and loosen your grip on their name; you can pick it back up later if you need to.

wordCard.voice: Rama's calm, toward blame. He tells Lakshmana not to blame Kaikeyi, calling what happened daiva, something larger than any one person.

orig.note: Sanskrit daiva: what comes from the devas, the gods; fate, destiny. Rama's word for what has happened.

carryVoice: Your line: daiva: larger than anyone's fault. Next week, Sita has something to say. Day five hundred twenty-five, done.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 22 (Rama to Lakshmana on daiva; not blaming Kaikeyi)
